name: Hagia Sophia
label: Hagia Sophia
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sultanahmet Meydanı' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Sultanahmet Meydanı' (way/25512790): middle (387 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/109862851: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Hagia Sophia' (215 m across).
notes: Byzantine cathedral turned mosque with a huge dome.

text.description:
Hagia Sophia is the great domed building at the heart of old Istanbul. Emperor Justinian I had it built between 532 and 537 as a church, and Isidore of Miletus and Anthemius of Tralles designed it. When it was finished it was the largest interior space in the world, and its dome design shaped later mosques across the city. It served as a church until 1453, then as a mosque, then as a museum from 1935 to 2020, and it is a mosque again today. That long history shows in the outline: a huge central dome, stepped semi-domes and minarets added later.

It photographs well from Sultanahmet Meydanı, the square beside it. From there the fountain gives you a foreground, and Hagia Sophia sits behind it with the Blue Mosque sometimes in the same frame. After dark the fountain lighting and the lit building add to the picture.

The square is crowded in the daytime and busiest after about 9 am, so go early if you can. Just after dawn the water is calmer and can give reflections. For a quieter alternative, the lantern-lined path by Hürrem Sultan Hamamı leads towards the big dome, though the whole building is harder to fit in. Keep your phone steady against your body or a railing, and wipe the lens before you start.
text.geographic_location: Hagia Sophia is in Sultanahmet, the old part of Istanbul, beside Sultanahmet Square. The Blue Mosque is nearby and can sometimes be framed together with Hagia Sophia.
text.directions_text: No tram or Underground stop is listed for this spot, so navigate to Sultanahmet Meydanı in the old city. From there Hagia Sophia lies about 400 m to the north-east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the fountain, Hagia Sophia and perhaps the Blue Mosque together. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view of Hagia Sophia past the fountain. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the dome and minarets, or to pick out details when the square is busy.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Sultanahmet Meydanı (central fountain, Hagia Sophia side of the square). Hagia Sophia framed past the fountain, with the Blue Mosque sometimes in the same frame, and the fountain lighting in the foreground after dark. By the central fountain on the Hagia Sophia side of the square. Hagia Sophia is to the north-east. From here the fountain forms the foreground, with Hagia Sophia framed behind it and the Blue Mosque sometimes beside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the fountain on the lower third, with Hagia Sophia above it. Keep the dome near the centre of the frame and hold the phone level so the minarets do not lean. For a different angle, try the three-quarter view from the corner of the square, which suits a night shot with the fountains in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and floodlit walls keep their detail. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body. The fountain lights change colour, so take a few frames.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Just after dawn, when the square is quiet and the water can reflect the building. After dark is the other good time, for the floodlit facade.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but Hagia Sophia is a mosque with its own visiting rules, and entry arrangements have changed in recent years, so check the official site before you go.

name: Grand Bazaar
label: Grand Bazaar
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.

notes: One of the world's largest covered markets.

text.description: The Grand Bazaar (Kapalıçarşı, 'Covered Market') is one of the largest and oldest covered markets in the world. It has 61 covered streets and over 4,000 shops across roughly 30,700 square metres. Its oldest part, the Old Bedesten, was begun in the winter of 1455/56, soon after the Ottoman conquest of the city, and the market grew up around it over the following centuries. For photographs, it is all about repeating patterns and colour. Hanging lamps, stacked ceramics, rugs, spices and painted vaults fill every frame, and the long, arched passages pull the eye down the street. The phone icon on the map is in the middle of the bazaar, so the subject is all around you rather than in one direction. Look for a straight stretch of passage and use the vaulted roof as your frame. Then step in closer to a single shopfront, a lamp display or a tray of tea glasses. Ask before photographing people. Keep a few moments for simple details such as tiles, lanterns and brass, which often look better than the wide view.
text.geographic_location: In the Fatih district of the old walled city of Istanbul, in the neighbourhood that shares its name. It stretches roughly from west to east between the Beyazıt Mosque and the Nuruosmaniye Mosque.
text.directions_text: From Sultanahmet or Sirkeci, the easiest way is the tram to the Beyazıt-Kapalıçarşı stop, then a short walk into the market. Once inside, the phone icon on the map is near the middle of the complex, so follow the main covered passages towards the centre. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the vaulted ceilings and long passages. Use the default lens (1x) for most shopfronts and street scenes. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as lamps, ceramics and spices from a polite distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The market surrounds you on every side, so there is no single building to aim at. Choose a straight passage and point your phone along it, keeping to the side so you do not block the flow of people.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the centre of the arched passage with the middle of the frame, so the vault repeats on both sides. Keep the phone level so the walls do not lean. For detail shots, fill the frame with one colourful display and include a little of the passage behind it for depth.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the brightest part of a display, then lower the exposure slider a little so lamps and glass do not burn out. If it is dim, use night mode and hold still for a second or two. Wipe the lens before you start, as bags and pockets leave smudges.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit when it is less crowded, if you can, so you have more room to frame a clean view down a passage.

text.access_note: This is a covered market with shops, and opening days and times can vary, so check the official site before you go.

name: Blue Mosque
label: Blue Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Seven Hills Restaurant' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Seven Hills Restaurant' (node/3090853853): point; moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/18055570: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Blue Mosque' (179 m across).
notes: Six-minaret mosque facing Hagia Sophia.

text.description:
The Blue Mosque, officially the Sultan Ahmed Mosque, is the Ottoman imperial mosque that gives the Sultanahmet neighbourhood its name. It was built between 1609 and 1617 for Sultan Ahmed I, on the old Hippodrome site and facing Hagia Sophia. Its outline is easy to recognise: a central dome stepping down through semi-domes and smaller domes, with six slim minarets around it. The prayer hall's central dome is 23.5 metres across. Inside, thousands of Iznik tiles in mostly blue tones gave the mosque its popular name. It joined the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1985 as part of the 'Historic Areas of Istanbul', and it reopened in April 2023 after a long restoration.

It photographs well from above, because a higher view shows the whole mosque, its domes and its minarets together. The rooftop terrace of Seven Hills Restaurant is a recommended elevated viewpoint. From there you can look over the rooftops with the Blue Mosque and Hagia Sophia side by side, plus the Sea of Marmara. Keep the horizon level with the gridlines and leave a little sky above the minarets. If you prefer street level, Sultanahmet Arkeolojik Park gives you the fountain in the foreground with the domes behind it, and Sultanahmet Meydanı frames the mosque with the German Fountain in front.
text.geographic_location: In the Sultanahmet area of Istanbul's old city, on the south-east side of the former Hippodrome and directly across from Hagia Sophia.
text.directions_text: Seven Hills Restaurant's rooftop terrace (Tevkifhane Sokak 8/A) is a suggested elevated viewpoint if you want a higher view. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the mosque and Hagia Sophia side by side. Then zoom to 2x-5x, depending on your phone, for a tighter shot of the domes and minarets. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the whole skyline, as it makes the mosque look smaller and further away.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Seven Hills Restaurant (rooftop terrace, Tevkifhane Sokak 8/A). An elevated view over the rooftops with the Blue Mosque and Hagia Sophia side by side, plus the Sea of Marmara. For an elevated alternative, try the rooftop terrace of Seven Hills Restaurant (Tevkifhane Sokak 8/A). From that height you see the whole mosque, with its domes and minarets, next to Hagia Sophia, plus the Sea of Marmara.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the main dome on a vertical third. Keep the minarets upright and leave a little sky above them. Hagia Sophia can fill the other side of the frame. For a street-level alternative, try Sultanahmet Arkeolojik Park, with the fountain in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the mosque to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the domes keep their detail. Try a panorama along the rooftops, moving slowly, to take in the whole skyline.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is a good bet, as the sun is then behind you and lights the mosque's face. In the evening you will be shooting towards the sun, so the mosque may come out darker.

text.access_note: The rooftop is part of a restaurant, so you are expected to order something, and it may be closed in winter; check the official site before you go. The mosque itself is closed to non-worshippers around the five daily prayers, and the park and square are open-air.
claims_not_in_sources: From the stand-here point the mosque is to the west, so morning sun comes from behind the photographer and evening sun shines towards the camera.
The 0.5x ultra-wide lens makes distant buildings look smaller in the frame.
A panorama taken slowly along the rooftops can capture the whole skyline.

name: Topkapı Palace
label: Topkapı Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bâb-ı Hümâyun' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Bâb-ı Hümâyûn' (way/335364925): middle (56 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Topkapı Palace'.
notes: Former Ottoman sultans' palace above the Bosphorus.

text.description:
Topkapı Palace sits on a hilly promontory above the water and was the main home and administrative centre of the Ottoman sultans from the 1460s until the mid-19th century. Mehmed the Conqueror ordered its construction in 1459, a few years after the conquest of Constantinople. The name Topkapı, meaning Cannon Gate, came into use after the early Ottoman period (dated to either the 18th or the 19th century). Since 1924 it has been a museum, and it forms part of the Historic Areas of Istanbul, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

For a phone photo, start at the front. The monumental stone entrance gate, Bâb-ı Hümâyun, is a strong, symmetrical subject, and with Hagia Sophia behind you it makes a good opening shot for the visit. Stand directly in front of the gate, switch on gridlines and line up the centre of the archway with the middle of the screen. As general photo advice, you can wait a moment for people to move through, or include a few of them to show how big the gate is.

Inside, the palace has four main courtyards and many smaller buildings. Two other views are popular with visitors: the Fourth Courtyard, with a wide panorama over the Bosphorus, Golden Horn, Galata Tower and the Asian shore, and the Baghdad Pavilion, with its blue-and-white tiles. Both are inside the ticketed grounds, so check the official site before you go, including whether those terraces are open that day.
text.geographic_location: Topkapı Palace is in the east of the Fatih district of Istanbul, on Seraglio Point (Sarayburnu), the promontory overlooking the Golden Horn where the Bosphorus meets the Sea of Marmara. The main gate faces Hagia Sophia.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or ferry stop is given for this spot, so head for Hagia Sophia in the Fatih district. Walk toward the palace; the main gate, Bâb-ı Hümâyun, is the palace entrance, and Hagia Sophia is directly behind you as you face it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the gate, as it keeps the straight lines and symmetry natural. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are too close to fit the whole gate in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details on the upper part of the gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (Standing directly in front of the main gate, with Hagia Sophia behind you). The monumental stone entrance gate of the palace, framed symmetrically, usually as an opening shot. Walk north-east toward the palace and, once you reach Bâb-ı Hümâyun, stand directly in front of the main gate with Hagia Sophia behind you. From there the photo shows the monumental stone gate framed symmetrically.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the archway on the centre line, keeping the phone level so the walls do not lean. Keep a little space above the gate. If you go inside the ticketed grounds, the Fourth Courtyard gives a wide Bosphorus and Golden Horn panorama, often with kiosk roofs in front. The Baghdad Pavilion gives a close-up of its blue-and-white tiles with the Golden Horn and Galata Tower behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gate to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its detail. As general advice, take a few frames while people cross the entrance. Tripods are not permitted and drones are banned, so hold the phone steady with both hands.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No best time is given for this spot. Check the official site for closing days before you plan the visit.

text.access_note: The gate viewpoint is listed as free, but the courtyard terraces inside need admission, and the palace is a museum with closing days, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Gridlines and lowering the exposure help keep a symmetrical, bright-sky gate shot level and detailed.
Waiting for people to move through, or including a few of them to show scale, is general photo advice.

name: Taksim Square
label: Taksim Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Taksim Meydanı' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Taksim Meydanı' (relation/4473230): middle (473 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/4473230: 'Republic Monument', the best-known feature inside 'Istanbul Taksim Square' (475 m across).
notes: Central square with the Republic Monument.

text.description: Taksim Square is the busy open plaza at the heart of modern Istanbul, in the Beyoğlu district, and its best-known feature is the Republic Monument. The sculptor Pietro Canonica made it, and it was inaugurated in 1928 to mark five years since the Republic of Turkey was founded in 1923. It works well as a photo subject because it stands on its own in the middle of a wide space, so you can frame it cleanly against the sky and the buildings around it. The Taksim Mosque, which opened in 2021, stands on the west side of the square and can add a second landmark to your frame. The Atatürk Cultural Centre also faces the square and reopened in 2021 after renovation. The name Taksim means 'division' or 'distribution'. The square was once where the city's main water lines were gathered and sent on to other districts. Several major roads meet here, and İstiklal Caddesi, the long pedestrian street, ends at the square, so there are plenty of people about. Be quick with your shots, or you will end up photographing strangers. You could also try the edge of Gezi Park for a quieter, wider look across the plaza, but this view is not confirmed, so check what it looks like on the day.
text.geographic_location: Taksim Square is in Beyoğlu, on the European side of Istanbul. Gezi Park lies to its north and the Taksim Mosque to its west, and İstiklal Caddesi begins at its edge.
text.directions_text: Head for Taksim Square in Beyoğlu, a major transport hub with a metro station and a funicular from Kabataş. If you are already on İstiklal Caddesi, simply walk to the end of the avenue, where the square opens up. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the monument with the wider square around it. Switch to the telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) to bring the mosque closer to the monument in the frame and cut out some of the crowd. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the whole plaza, and expect the monument to look small in it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Taksim Meydanı (on the south side of the Republic Monument, facing the monument with the Taksim Mosque behind it). The Republic Monument in the middle of the square, with the Taksim Mosque rising in the background. The Taksim Mosque is on the west side of the square, so it will sit to one side of or beyond the monument rather than directly behind it. Step a little left or right until the mosque sits neatly beside or beyond the monument rather than growing out of it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the monument on one of the vertical lines, with the mosque in the space to one side if it fits. Keep the phone level so the buildings do not lean. Take your shot in a quiet moment between groups of people. For an alternative, you could try the view from the edge of Gezi Park looking across the plaza, though this is not confirmed, so check it on the day.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the monument to set focus and exposure, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky looks washed out. Take several frames in a row, because people keep walking through the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the day if you can, when there are fewer people in the square. After rain, wet paving can give pleasing reflections, so try a low phone angle then.

text.access_note: Taksim Square is an open public space, but access can be restricted around certain dates, so check the official site or local news before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early in the day the square usually has fewer people than later on.
A telephoto lens (2x-3x) compresses the distance between the monument and the mosque.
Moving a little left or right changes how the Taksim Mosque lines up with the monument.
Wet paving after rain can give reflections (suggested by guides).
The edge of Gezi Park may give a quieter, wider view across the plaza (not confirmed in sources; check on site).

name: Galata Tower
label: Galata Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Büyük Hendek Caddesi' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Büyük Hendek Caddesi nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23236783: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Galata Tower' (24 m across).
notes: Medieval stone tower with city views.

text.description:
Galata Tower is a round stone tower of 62.59 m that stands on the hill above the Golden Horn in Beyoğlu. The Genoese built it in the 14th century as the main tower of their fortifications at Galata, and it has been a watchtower, a fire lookout and a tourist attraction. Since 2020 it has been a museum and exhibition venue. It has 11 floors, a Romanesque design and a conical roof.

The classic ground-level photo is taken from Büyük Hendek Caddesi. The tower rises at the top of a sloping street, with old facades, shopfronts and café awnings on either side. These act as a natural frame and lead the eye up to the tower, which makes the picture feel like Istanbul rather than a plain shot of a monument. Crowds gather here in the afternoon, so an early start makes it much easier to get a clear view.

If you want a different view, Galata Bridge shows the tower above the Karaköy rooftops, with the Golden Horn, fishing lines and ferries in the foreground. Tersane Caddesi shows it against open sky, away from the crowds. You do not need to go up the tower for these pictures.
text.geographic_location: Galata Tower is in the Galata neighbourhood of Beyoğlu, on the hill north of the Golden Horn. Büyük Hendek Caddesi is the sloping street that leads up to it.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot; head to the Galata neighbourhood in Beyoğlu and look for Galata Tower. Büyük Hendek Caddesi, the street that climbs towards the tower, is the classic viewpoint. Standing farther back along it gives the framed view of the tower at the top of the street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the tower and the street frame together. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is too narrow to fit the facades in, or if you are close to the tower's base. Try the telephoto or zoom (2x-3x) to bring the tower closer and keep passers-by out of the corners.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Büyük Hendek Caddesi (stand partway down the street and face the tower at its upper end). The tower rises at the end of a sloping street, framed by old facades, shopfronts and café awnings. For that view, stand farther back along the street and face the tower at its upper end, with old facades, shopfronts and café awnings on either side.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and centre the tower between the two rows of buildings, keeping the phone level so the street edges look straight. Leave a little room above the roof. Waiting a moment for a gap in the crowd helps. For a different view, Galata Bridge or Tersane Caddesi are good alternatives.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to set focus and exposure, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out and the roof keeps its detail. Hold the phone steady with both hands.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or just after sunrise, when the street is calmer and the light is softer. Afternoons are busier.

text.access_note: The street is open to the public, but the tower is a museum with a ticket-control area, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.
claims_not_in_sources: Tilting the phone upwards on a narrow street can make the tower look as if it leans, so keeping the phone level helps.
Lowering the exposure slider can stop a bright sky from washing out the picture.
The tower lies to the east of the stand-here point, so the early light may fall on the street at an angle.

name: Süleymaniye Mosque
label: Süleymaniye Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Süleymaniye Mosque' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1564032: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Süleymaniye Mosque' (179 m across).
notes: Sinan's imperial mosque on the third hill.

text.description:
The Süleymaniye Mosque sits on the Third Hill of Istanbul and looks out over the Golden Horn. Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent commissioned it, and the imperial architect Mimar Sinan designed it. An inscription gives 1550 as the foundation date and 1557 as the inauguration date. It is the largest Ottoman-era mosque in the city and part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site 'Historic Areas of Istanbul'. Behind the prayer hall is a walled cemetery with the separate mausoleums of Suleiman and his wife Hurrem Sultan.

For a phone photo, the outer courtyard is a calm place to start. The symmetrical colonnade and the domes sit behind a row of arches, and the arches make natural frames. Beyond the courtyard wall you can see the Golden Horn. The courtyard is a quieter, more geometric alternative to the Blue Mosque's courtyard, and a good choice if the terrace is crowded or closed.

Stand among the corner arches and use them as a frame around the domes. Switch on gridlines so the columns and rooflines stay straight. Take one wide shot to show the whole courtyard, then move closer for details of the stonework. The mosque is an active place of worship, so photograph the exterior and courtyard outside prayer times, keep the flash off and dress modestly. Late afternoon is the best time, when the stone takes on a warm glow.
text.geographic_location: The mosque is on the Third Hill of Istanbul's Historic Peninsula, in the old city above the Golden Horn. It is part of a larger külliye complex that included madrasas, a public kitchen and a hospital.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed close to this spot, so head for the Third Hill on the Historic Peninsula, above the Golden Horn, and navigate to Süleymaniye Camii. Once you arrive, walk into the outer courtyard and stop among the corner arches. From the Galata Bridge you can see the mosque's domes and minarets on the hill across the Golden Horn. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole courtyard and several arches at once. Use the default lens (1x) for the cleanest, most symmetrical view of the colonnade and domes. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out a single dome or the Golden Horn beyond the wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the symmetrical colonnade and domes are framed by the arches, with the Golden Horn visible beyond the wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Step back until an arch makes a frame around the dome, and use the gridlines to keep the columns upright. Stand in the centre of the courtyard for a symmetrical shot, or move to a corner for a diagonal view through the arches. If you want a different view, the Galata Bridge shows the domes and minarets on the hill across the Golden Horn.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone of the colonnade to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky stays blue and the domes keep their detail. Keep the flash off.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the stone glows. Avoid prayer times.

text.access_note: This is an active place of worship, so dress modestly and avoid prayer times; check the official site before you go, as access to the courtyard and terrace may vary.

name: Basilica Cistern
label: Basilica Cistern
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/11006008339: the OpenStreetMap point 'Basilica Cistern (Exit)'.
notes: Underground Byzantine water reservoir with columns.

text.description: The Basilica Cistern is an underground chamber beneath the old city, built in the 6th century under the Byzantine emperor Justinian I. It is the largest of several hundred ancient cisterns under Istanbul. It measures roughly 138 by 65 metres, and its roof is held up by a forest of 336 marble columns, each about 9 metres high. They stand in 12 rows of 28. Most of the columns were reused from older buildings, and the capitals are mainly Ionic and Corinthian, with a few plain Doric. That regular repetition is what makes the place work in a photo: rows of columns fade into the dark, with a little shallow water below. Two column bases in the north-west corner reuse blocks carved with Medusa's face, a distinctive detail worth a close-up. The cistern was opened to the public as a museum in 1987. It was restored again between 2020 and 2022 and has a new walkway that stays separate from the old structure. Inside it is dim and atmospheric, so expect low light and slow-moving queues at the best corners. Keep your phone steady, shoot a few frames of each view and check them as you go. Rules on photography and access can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the old city of Istanbul, on the historical peninsula of Sarayburnu, about 150 metres south-west of Hagia Sophia. The visit is underground, below a busy historic area.
text.directions_text: Start from Hagia Sophia, the best-known landmark nearby. The cistern lies about 150 metres to its south-west. If you are coming from elsewhere in the city, head for the Hagia Sophia area first and walk the last stretch. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to catch the rows of columns running away from you. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view along one row. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the Medusa column base and for carved capitals.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up one row of columns so it runs towards the middle of the frame. Keep the walkway rail out of the corners where you can. For the Medusa heads in the north-west corner, step in close with telephoto and keep the face upright and sharp. Take a few frames of each view, because other visitors will drift through.

label: Spice Bazaar
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mısır Çarşısı' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Mısır Çarşısı' (way/24234971): middle (229 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.

text.description:
The Spice Bazaar, known in Turkish as Mısır Çarşısı, is one of the largest bazaars in Istanbul and the most famous covered shopping complex after the Grand Bazaar. It was built from 1660, after the Great Fire of that year, as part of the complex around the New Mosque. Rents from its shops helped pay for the mosque's upkeep. Today it has 85 shops selling spices, Turkish delight and other sweets, jewellery, souvenirs, and dried fruits and nuts.

The best exterior photo is at the main entrance archway. The tiled arch makes a natural frame, and the colourful goods on display and the market's facade sit behind it. Inside, a second good picture looks down the crossing aisles, with piles of spice and shoppers filling the frame. If you have time, Eminönü Meydanı gives a raised view of the New Mosque forecourt and Galata Bridge together. The bazaar is only a short walk away, but it is not the main subject from there.

Many stalls have 'no photography' signs, so choose spots without them. Ask before photographing vendors up close, and note that some guides say a tip or a purchase is expected. Guides generally suggest early morning for the softest light, but check on the day for exactly which hour is best.
text.geographic_location: The Spice Bazaar is in the Eminönü quarter of the Fatih district, in Istanbul. It belongs to the complex of the New Mosque.

text.description:
Dolmabahçe Palace is a long, pale waterfront palace on the European shore of the Bosphorus. It was ordered by Sultan Abdülmecid I and built between 1843 and 1853. It is the largest palace in Turkey, with 285 rooms and 46 halls. Its design mixes Baroque, Rococo and Neoclassical touches with Ottoman tradition. It served as the main administrative centre of the Ottoman Empire for long periods, and Atatürk died here in 1938.

From a phone's point of view, the palace works best as a wide, calm frame. The sea-facing facade runs in a long, even line, and ferries and ships crossing the Bosphorus add movement and scale. The easiest place for the full waterfront is the pier to the south, with the palace stretching away ahead of you. A short stroll along the promenade gives you different angles of the same facade, so it is worth taking a few steps between shots.

If you go inside the grounds, there are two other good pictures: the ornate Bosphorus Gates with the water and the Asian shore behind, and the symmetrical Imperial Gate (also called the Sultanate Gate) centred in the frame. Interior photography has been restricted, so ask an attendant before you take any pictures inside, and check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In Istanbul, on the European shore of the Bosphorus, with the sea along its eastern side. The pier at Kabataş is on the waterfront promenade south of the palace, about 960 m away.

name: Maiden's Tower

camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sarayburnu' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Sarayburnu' (node/11514193965): point.

text.description:
The Maiden's Tower (Kız Kulesi) stands on a small islet at the southern entrance of the Bosphorus, about 200 m off the Üsküdar shore. From Sarayburnu, on the European side, you see it across open water. The tower is small in the frame, with the strait around it, so this is the photo that shows the tower in its setting rather than filling the picture. The water, the sky and any passing boats do much of the work.

The tower has been rebuilt many times. A wooden tower was built here in 1110 under the Byzantine emperor Alexius Comnenus. The tower was destroyed in the 1509 earthquake and burned down in 1721. In 1763 it was rebuilt in more durable stone. It was restored again between 2021 and 2023 and reopened to the public in May 2023. It is also called Leander's Tower, and there are several stories about where the name comes from, including one about an emperor's daughter and a snake.

Because the tower is small from here, don't expect a close-up. Put the tower off-centre, leave plenty of water around it, and keep the horizon level. If you want the tower larger, with the Historic Peninsula's domes and minarets behind it, Salacak İskelesi is the usual alternative. Nakkaştepe Park gives a higher view of the tower against the European skyline.

If you prefer a closer shot, with the tower in front and the Historic Peninsula's domes and minarets behind it, the alternative is Salacak İskelesi.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the tower on one of the crossing points rather than in the middle. Keep the horizon on a gridline so it stays level. Leave open water around the tower so it looks like it sits on its own islet. Use a boat or a ferry passing through the strait to add scale.

text.description: The Chora Church, also called Kariye Mosque (Kariye Camii), is a Byzantine church in the Edirnekapı neighbourhood of Fatih. It is best known for its Late Byzantine mosaics and wall paintings. Most of the building you see dates from the late 11th century, when it was rebuilt on a cross-in-square plan. Much of the decoration was paid for by the statesman Theodore Metochites, with the interior work carried out between about 1310 and 1317. It is small compared with other Byzantine churches in the city, at about 742 square metres, which makes it easy to take in on foot. From the outside it photographs as a cluster of old brick walls, rounded forms and domes, with a brick minaret added when it became a mosque around 1500. The church later served as a museum from 1945 and became a mosque again in 2020, opening for worship in May 2024. Because of this, what you can see and photograph inside may differ from older guidebooks. For the exterior, walk slowly around the building and look for angles where the domes and the minaret sit together. Include a little of the surrounding street or trees to give a sense of place. Keep your phone level, switch on gridlines so the walls stay straight, and take a few frames from different sides. If you plan to go inside, check the official site before you go for current visiting rules, including whether photography is allowed.
text.geographic_location: The Chora Church is in the Edirnekapı neighbourhood of the western Fatih district of Istanbul, on a slope that runs down towards the north. It stands near the line of the old Theodosian walls. It was first built outside them, and the walls later enclosed it.

text.description: This open square in Istanbul's old city was once the Hippodrome of Constantinople, the sporting and social centre of the Eastern Roman Empire. Chariot races were held here, and the track was roughly 450 m long and 130 m wide, with stands for around 100,000 people. Most of the stadium has gone, but some of the monuments that stood along its central barrier are still in place. The best known is the pink granite obelisk that Theodosius brought from Egypt in AD 390. It was first raised at Karnak in about 1490 BC. Its carved base shows the emperor and the race in progress, which makes it the natural subject for a close photo. The Serpent Column, cast to mark a Greek victory over the Persians in the 5th century BC, stands nearby. Its serpent heads were destroyed in 1700. The photo works because you get old stone in the foreground and the Blue Mosque's domes and minarets behind it, all in one frame. Walk up to the base first and photograph the carvings, then step back and take the wider view with the mosque. In April the tulip beds add colour, according to one guide. Spring and autumn are the busiest seasons, so go early if you want fewer people in the shot.
text.geographic_location: The spot is Sultanahmet Square (Sultanahmet Meydanı) in the old city of Istanbul. It sits on the line of the old Hippodrome, close to the Blue Mosque.

shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning before 9 AM, or late afternoon, for soft light and fewer people. The Blue Mosque makes a good backdrop at sunset. Spring and autumn are the busiest seasons. Summer midday can be hot and crowded.

text.description: The 15 July Martyrs Bridge, still widely called the Bosphorus Bridge or the First Bridge, is the oldest and southernmost of the three suspension bridges across the strait. It links Ortaköy on the European side with Beylerbeyi on the Asian side. It was finished on 30 October 1973 and is about 1,560 m long. Its two steel towers are 165 m tall, and the main span between them is 1,074 m. The bridge was renamed in 2016 in memory of those killed during the coup attempt that July. It photographs well because the deck seems to float across the water, and the towers give a strong shape against the sky. Since 2007 the bridge has also been lit at night by colour-changing lights. For a phone photo, the quieter Asian shore near Beylerbeyi Sarayı works well. From there you can put the palace in the foreground and let the bridge rise behind it. The bridge carries vehicles only, and stopping or walking on it is not allowed, so take your photos from the shore or from a Bosphorus boat. If you prefer the European side, Ortaköy has the small mosque in front of the bridge. Keep the horizon level and leave a little sky above the towers.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bridge to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on a wall or railing to keep the lights sharp.

text.description:
İstiklal Avenue is one of Istanbul's most famous avenues, a pedestrian street 1.4 kilometres long through the Beyoğlu (Pera) district from Taksim Square down to Tünel Square. It photographs well because it is one long, lively corridor lined with late Ottoman buildings in Neo-Classical, Neo-Gothic, Art Nouveau and other styles. A red nostalgic tram runs down the middle, so you get a ready-made focal point. The street took its name, meaning 'Independence', after the Republic was declared on 29 October 1923. The trams came back in 1990, when the street was pedestrianised and restored.

The classic frame is from the Taksim end. The Republic Monument gives you a strong foreground, and the street runs downhill behind it. Wait for the tram to come into the gap, then take a few shots. If you want something quieter, the entrance to the Çiçek Pasajı (Flower Passage) gives a different view, with ironwork and a glass roof inside and the street outside. At the far end, Tünel Square has the avenue climbing away from you and the tram line in view. It is also the place to try for the Galata Tower area, which is not visible from the avenue itself. Expect crowds, so keep your phone in hand and be ready for passing people to fill the frame.

text.description:
Galata Bridge crosses the Golden Horn between Karaköy on the north shore and Eminönü on the south. The one you see today is the fifth bridge on this site, finished in December 1994. It is named after Galata, the old name for Karaköy. The first bridge here was a wooden one from 1845, and a floating bridge of 1912 later carried the crossing for decades. Back in 1502–1503 Leonardo da Vinci drew up a single-span design for this stretch of water, but the Sultan did not approve it.

The bridge photographs well because the whole scene lines up. The bridge, the water and the domes and minarets sit in clear layers, which suits a phone camera. Switch on gridlines and set the bridge's line along a lower third, with the mosques filling the space above it.

If you would rather have a closer, busier picture, walk onto the bridge itself. There the upper deck has fishermen along the railings, with the Süleymaniye Mosque on the skyline beyond the Golden Horn. Check the signs on the day, as walking arrangements on the bridge can change.
text.geographic_location: Galata Bridge is in central Istanbul, linking Karaköy in the Beyoğlu district with Eminönü in the Fatih district across the Golden Horn.
text.directions_text: Head for Karaköy, on the north side of the Golden Horn, by public transport or on foot, and make your way to the waterfront at Karaköy Balık Pazarı. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the bridge, the water and the mosque skyline in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the mosques closer behind the bridge.

The bridge spanning the water toward Eminönü, with the New Mosque and Süleymaniye Mosque rising behind it. name: New Mosque
label: New Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Eminönü Meydanı' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Eminönü Meydanı' (relation/4800787): middle (496 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/7574356: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'New Mosque' (125 m across).

text.description:
The New Mosque (Yeni Cami) sits right on the Golden Horn at the southern end of the Galata Bridge, and its stack of domes makes it one of the easiest buildings in Eminönü to photograph. The domes and semi-domes rise in a pyramid shape, 66 in all, with two minarets beside them. The main dome is 36 metres high. In front is a large courtyard, 39 metres along each side, ringed by a colonnade with 24 small domes. Work began in 1597 for Safiye Sultan, stalled after 1603, and restarted in 1660 under Turhan Sultan. The mosque was finished in 1663 and opened in 1665. Its first name was the Valide Sultan Mosque, and 'New Mosque' stuck as the everyday name.

For your photo, go to Eminönü Meydanı and find the raised platform at the northeast corner, near the tram stop. From up there you look over the forecourt with the Galata Bridge in the same frame. It is a quieter spot than the bridge itself, and many people walk straight past it. Start with a wide shot that shows the domes, the forecourt and the bridge together. Then move in for a tighter picture of the dome stack. Go early if you can, as the square is calmer. The square fills up around Friday midday prayers, so avoid that time. Please don't take close-ups of worshippers without asking.
text.geographic_location: In the Eminönü quarter of Istanbul's old city, on the Golden Horn at the southern end of the Galata Bridge. It stands beside the Spice Bazaar, which was built as part of the same complex.
text.directions_text: Make your way to Eminönü, at the southern end of the Galata Bridge. Look for the northeast corner of Eminönü Meydanı, where a raised platform stands near the tram stop. From there the mosque is to the south-east, about 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to get the forecourt, the mosque and the Galata Bridge into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the domes and minarets.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Eminönü Meydanı (northeast corner, on the raised platform near the tram stop). An elevated view of the mosque's forecourt with the Galata Bridge in the same frame. At the northeast corner on the raised platform near the tram stop. The mosque is to the south-east. From this slightly higher spot you look over the mosque's forecourt, with the Galata Bridge in the same frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the domes on the upper line and the bridge on a side line. Keep the horizon level, because the mosque's outline looks best when the verticals are straight. If the platform is busy, wait for a gap rather than leaning over people. For a different view, try the Galata Bridge, where you can catch the mosque rising over the Eminönü waterfront with the road and bridge in front and the Golden Horn beside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the domes to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky doesn't wash out the stonework. Take a few frames at each zoom level, as it is hard to judge the framing on a bright screen.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the square is quieter. Avoid Friday around midday prayers, when the square fills up.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship and is closed to tourists during extended Friday midday prayers, so check the official site before you go and dress respectfully if you plan to go inside.
claims_not_in_sources: Gridlines and a slight downward exposure adjustment can help with a bright sky behind the domes.
Modest dress is expected when visiting an active mosque.
The ultra-wide lens helps to fit a large building and a bridge into one frame from a busy square.

label: Ortaköy Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ortaköy İskelesi' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Ortaköy İskelesi' (way/244145656): middle (27 m across); moved 10 m off water.

text.description: Ortaköy Mosque sits right on the water's edge in the Ortaköy pier square, in front of the Bosphorus Bridge. That mix of a small, richly carved mosque, moving water and a huge bridge is why it is photographed so often. The mosque is formally the Büyük Mecidiye Camii. Sultan Abdülmecid I commissioned it, and it was finished around 1854 or 1856. The architects were the Armenian father and son Garabet and Nikoğos Balyan, who also designed Dolmabahçe Palace nearby. It has a single dome and two slim minarets. The stone carving on its walls is unusually ornate for a mosque of its period. It was restored over three years and reopened in 2014. The bridge behind it is officially the 15 July Martyrs Bridge. From the pier you see the mosque front-on with the bridge off to the right, a different angle from the square, and a good option when the square is crowded. The square itself gives a second view, with the mosque in the foreground, the bridge rising behind one minaret and small boats on the water. Keep the whole mosque in the frame, including a little water and sky, so the bridge has room to appear. Take a few shots at different times if you are staying nearby, because the light changes the mood a lot.
text.geographic_location: Ortaköy Mosque is in the Ortaköy district of Beşiktaş, on the European shore of the Bosphorus. It stands at the waterside of the pier square, close to the Bosphorus Bridge.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Head for the small pier where the short Bosphorus cruises leave. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the mosque front-on. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the mosque, water and bridge all in one frame. Try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carved details and the minarets.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Ortaköy İskelesi (walk out toward the ferry ticket kiosks and turn back toward the mosque). The mosque seen front-on with the bridge off to the right, a different angle from the square. Walk out toward the ferry ticket kiosks and turn back toward the mosque, which lies to the east. You will see it straight on with the bridge off to the right, a different angle from the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the mosque on one side line, with the bridge on the other side. Keep the horizon level so the water edge does not tilt. For another angle, Ortaköy Meydanı (the square) shows the mosque in the foreground with the bridge rising behind one minaret and small boats passing.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the mosque to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the stone keeps its detail. If you shoot at dusk, try night mode and hold your phone against a railing or your body to keep it steady. Try a Live Photo to catch boats passing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the sun drops behind the Asian-side hills and softens the light on the European shore. Advice on timing varies: some people prefer sunrise, others sunset or dusk, when the bridge lights are on.

text.access_note: This is a working mosque, closed to visitors during Friday midday prayers, so check the official site before you go; the pier and square are public places by the water.

name: Hagia Irene
label: Hagia Irene
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Aya İrini Müzesi' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).

text.description:
Hagia Irene is a former Byzantine church standing in the outer courtyard of Topkapı Palace. Its name means "Holy Peace". It is the oldest known church structure in Istanbul, and one of only two Byzantine churches in the city that were never turned into mosques. After 1453 it was enclosed within the palace walls and used as an arsenal until the 19th century, which is why it was never converted into a mosque. The church was burned in the Nika revolt of 532 and rebuilt in 548 under Justinian I. It is now a museum and concert hall.

It photographs well because of its broad, plain brick walls and the way the roof steps up and down towards the dome. The phone icon on the map sits at the centre of the building's outline, so the best exterior view comes from stepping back to the west approach from the First Courtyard and taking in the whole side of the building. The courtyard setting also gives you trees and open sky to balance the heavy brickwork.

Take one wide shot of the whole exterior first. Then move in for details such as the arched windows and the junction of the different roof levels. If you go inside, you are looking for a high view of the nave and the cross mosaic in the apse. Entry to the museum is a separate matter, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Hagia Irene is in the outer courtyard of Topkapı Palace in Istanbul.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the First Courtyard of Topkapı Palace. Hagia Irene stands in that outer courtyard, and the phone icon on the map sits at the centre of the building's outline. Approach from the west side for the best view of the exterior. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the west approach so the whole brick exterior and dome fit in. Switch to the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the different roof heights without walking closer. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are tight against the wall, and keep the building straight in the frame so it does not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From there you see the broad brick exterior and the dome, and the varying roof heights read clearly. Approaching from the west also shows how the atrium, outer entrance and narthex relate to each other.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up a vertical wall edge with a grid line to keep the brickwork upright. Leave a band of sky above the dome and some courtyard ground below to give a sense of scale. For a second view, go inside the museum and shoot upwards to the nave and the cross mosaic in the apse. That view is indoors and needs museum admission.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brickwork to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. Keep the flash off indoors, as flash and tripods may be restricted. In the dim interior, night mode can help, but rest your elbows against something steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No fixed time is recommended. Soft light, either early or late in the day, usually flatters brick walls, and a quieter courtyard makes it easier to take a clear photo of the whole building.

text.access_note: The outer courtyard of Topkapı Palace is said by guides to be free to enter, so the exterior can be photographed from there, but the museum interior needs admission and opening days vary, so check the official site before you go.

text.description: Rüstem Pasha Mosque is a small Ottoman mosque in the streets of Tahtakale, close to the Spice Bazaar. It was designed by the imperial architect Mimar Sinan for Rüstem Pasha, a Grand Vizier under Suleiman I, and was finished around 1563. What makes it worth a photo is the colour. İznik tiles cover almost every vertical surface under the entrance porch, and inside there are roughly 2,300 of them in about 80 patterns. The mosque stands on a high terrace above a row of vaulted shops, so from the street you look up at a raised porch, with the busy market below and the quieter mosque above. It was used for film storage for a time and reopened for worship in 2021 after a long restoration. The mosque is to the north-east of that spot, and the stairs up to it start from this street. If you have time, the Eminönü seafront gives a wider view across the waterfront, and the Mısır Çarşısı side shows the mosque above the Spice Bazaar shops. The street is narrow and busy, so keep your phone close and step aside for passers-by.
text.geographic_location: Rüstem Pasha Mosque is in the Tahtakale neighbourhood of the Fatih district, in the Hasırcılar (strawmat weavers') market area near the Spice Bazaar.
text.directions_text: Head for the Spice Bazaar (Mısır Çarşısı) in Eminönü, then walk into the market streets of Tahtakale to Hasırcılar Caddesi. The mosque sits above the street, and the narrow stairs up to it start from Hasırcılar Caddesi. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole façade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is too tight to fit the porch in. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tile panels and the porch columns.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Hasırcılar Caddesi (west side, street view of the mosque and its north façade). The mosque's raised, tiled-porch façade seen from the street below, with the main entrance on the north side. From there the mosque's raised, tiled-porch façade rises above you to the north-east, with the main entrance on the north side.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the phone level, so the terrace and porch don't lean. Include a little of the shops below to show how the mosque sits above the market. For a different view, try the Eminönü seafront for the mosque across the waterfront, or the Mısır Çarşısı side for the mosque above the Spice Bazaar shops.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tiled porch to set focus, then pull the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky doesn't wash out the colours. If you go inside, turn the flash off.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the day, when the lanes are quieter and it is easier to stand back and get the whole façade in.

text.access_note: This is a working mosque, so dress modestly, take your shoes off inside, shoot without flash, and be respectful during prayer times; opening times can change, so check before you go.
